title: Humanity's First Killer App Was a Spreadsheet
subtitle: The earliest writing isn't poetry or scripture. It's receipts — lists of grain and sheep. And that boring origin explains everything.
hook: We picture writing beginning with an epic poem or a sacred law. Nope. The oldest writing on Earth is basically **accounting** — tallies of grain, sheep, and taxes owed. Disappointing? Only until you see *why*: once farming made surplus (yesterday's lesson), somebody had to track who stored what and who owed whom. Writing was invented to handle **information that outgrew human memory.** It was civilization's first killer app — and every tech leap since, right up to the internet, rhymes with it.

builds_on.label: The Worst Good Idea in History

sections.heading: From clay tokens to cuneiform
sections.body:
In ancient Mesopotamia, traders first tracked goods with little clay **tokens** — one shape per commodity. As trade grew, they pressed the tokens' marks into clay tablets, then simplified those marks into symbols. By ~3200 BCE this became **cuneiform** — wedge-shaped signs in clay. Egypt, China, and Mesoamerica each cooked up their own scripts, too. Independent invention again — same pattern as farming.

Crucially, early writing recorded *quantities and things*, not speech. Only later did symbols come to stand for **sounds** — and then writing could capture anything language could: names, laws, stories, ideas.

sections.caption: Same chain as yesterday: surplus → records to keep → the tech to keep them, evolving from tokens to a full writing system.

sections.label: Why it broke history open
sections.body: Writing let information escape a single skull. It could be **stored** longer than memory, **copied** and carried across distance, and **accumulated** across generations. Knowledge stopped dying with the knower. Every information technology since — the printing press, the telegraph, the computer, the internet — does those same three jobs (store, transmit, accumulate) at ever-bigger scale.

sections.label: And it minted power
sections.body: Whoever could write could **run things** — levy taxes, enforce contracts, issue laws, manage a bureaucracy bigger than any chief could hold in his head. Writing and the **state** grew up together, which is why literacy was long hoarded by a small scribe class. Control of information has meant power since the very first tablet.

sections.caption: How record-keeping became cuneiform — the birth of writing.

takeaways: The earliest writing was **accounting**, not literature — grain, sheep, taxes.
It arose to manage **surplus-driven information** beyond human memory (builds on the farming lesson).
It evolved tokens → marks → **cuneiform**, and was **independently invented** in several places.
Only later did symbols encode **sounds**, unlocking writing anything language can say.
Writing lets knowledge be **stored, copied, accumulated** — and hands power to whoever controls it.

quiz.q: What was most early writing actually used for?
quiz.explain: The oldest tablets are economic records. Writing was born to manage surplus-driven information.

quiz.q: The three jobs every info technology does (writing → internet)?
quiz.explain: Store beyond memory, transmit across distance, accumulate across generations.

quiz.q: CALLBACK: How does writing connect to the farming lesson?
options: Farming's surplus created goods and debts worth tracking — writing was the tool to track them
quiz.explain: Surplus → stuff to account for → writing. The History track is one chain: each lesson feeds the next.

tg_quiz.q: The world's oldest writing was mostly…
tg_quiz.correct: Right — receipts and tallies. History's first spreadsheet.
tg_quiz.wrong: It was accounting — grain, sheep, and taxes, not poetry.
tg_quiz.explain: Writing was invented to track surplus, not to tell stories.
